name: Question 5
worked_solution:
Notice that the quadratic factor in the denominator has a discriminant that is not a perfect square:

$$
D=(4)^{2}-4(1)(-6)=40
$$

We have that $\sqrt{40}$ is not a rational number, which implies that the quadratic factor doesn't factor over the rational numbers.

So, we proceed with the following partial fraction decomposition:

$$
\frac{4{x}^{2}+12x-12}{x({x}^{2}+4x-6)}=\frac{A}{x}+\frac{Bx+C}{{x}^{2}+4x-6}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $x({x}^{2}+4x-6),$ and we get

$$
4{x}^{2}+12x-12=A({x}^{2}+4x-6)+(Bx+C)x
$$

Solving for the unknown constants using the usual methods, we get $A=2,B=2$, and $C=4.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{4{x}^{2}+12x-12}{x({x}^{2}+4x-6)}=\frac{2}{x}+\frac{2x+4}{{x}^{2}+4x-6}.
$$

We now integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration at the very end.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4{x}^{2}+12x-12}{x({x}^{2}+4x-6)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{2}{x}+\frac{2x+4}{{x}^{2}+4x-6})\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{2x+4}{{x}^{2}+4x-6}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

For the first integral, we have

$$
\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|.
$$

For the second integral, we use the substitution $u={x}^{2}+4x-6.$ Then $\text{d}u=(2x+4)\,\text{d}x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x+4}{{x}^{2}+4x-6}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{u})\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u| \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{2}+4x-6|\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4{x}^{2}+12x-12}{x({x}^{2}+4x-6)}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{2x+4}{{x}^{2}+4x-6}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{2}+4x-6|+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Evaluate the integral ∫4x2+12x−12x(x2+4x−6)dx.

a
 2ln⁡|x|+1ln⁡|x2+4x−6|+K
b
 ln⁡|x|+12ln⁡|x2+4x−6|+K
c
 2x+ln⁡|x2+4x−6|+K
d
 2ln⁡|x|+ln⁡|x2+4x−6|+K
e
 3ln⁡|x|+13ln⁡|x2+4x−6|+K
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that the quadratic factor in the denominator has a discriminant that is not a perfect square: D=(4)2−4(1)(−6)=40 We have that 40 is not a rational number, which implies that the quadratic factor doesn't factor over the rational numbers.

So, we proceed with the following partial fraction decomposition: 4x2+12x−12x(x2+4x−6)=Ax+Bx+Cx2+4x−6

To determine the coefficients A,B, and C, we first multiply both sides of the above equation by x(x2+4x−6), and we get

4x2+12x−12=A(x2+4x−6)+(Bx+C)x

Solving for the unknown constants using the usual methods, we get A=2,B=2, and C=4. Therefore, 4x2+12x−12x(x2+4x−6)=2x+2x+4x2+4x−6.

We now integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration at the very end.

∫4x2+12x−12x(x2+4x−6)dx=∫(2x+2x+4x2+4x−6)dx=2∫1xdx+∫2x+4x2+4x−6dx.

For the first integral, we have ∫1xdx=ln⁡|x|.

For the second integral, we use the substitution u=x2+4x−6. Then du=(2x+4)dx, and we get ∫2x+4x2+4x−6dx=∫(1u)du=ln⁡|u|=ln⁡|x2+4x−6|

So, we get the following result: ∫4x2+12x−12x(x2+4x−6)dx=2∫1xdx+∫2x+4x2+4x−6dx=2ln⁡|x|+ln⁡|x2+4x−6|+K.
